title: How to Appear in "Best in My City" Questions
h1: How to appear in "best in my city" questions
desc: Local customers ask AI tools for the best business near them. Here is what a local business can do to be understood, with practical steps and honest limits.
lead: "Best [service] in [city]" is one of the most common questions customers ask. Nobody outside the platforms knows exactly how tools answer it, but you can make your business easy to understand and verify.
body:
Customers ask AI tools things like "best dentist in Jeddah" or "where to buy fresh coffee beans in Dubai". The answer usually names a few businesses. Here is what I would do so yours is a business the tool can understand and check. I cannot promise it will be named.

What I know and what I do not

I do not know how any tool ranks local businesses. The platforms do not publish it, and answers differ between runs, users and countries. What I can tell you comes from my work, and I label it as practice.

One documented point from Google: a page must be indexed and eligible to show a snippet to appear as a supporting link in its AI features, and normal search best practices apply.

Seven steps for a local business

  1. Say your category and city plainly. The first sentence of your homepage and service pages should state what you are and where: "Example Dental Clinic is a family dental clinic in Jeddah."
  2. Complete your Google Maps profile. Name, category, hours, services, photos and contact details, the same as on your website. At Point Market I manage the profiles of 37 branches, and the most common problems are small mismatches in hours and names.
  3. Make one page per service and per location. A page titled "Teeth whitening in Jeddah" answers the question better than a general page that mentions it once.
  4. Answer the question first. Start each service page with a direct answer, then add price ranges, process and conditions.
  5. Ask for reviews that name the service and city. A review that says "booked a whitening session at the Jeddah branch" is more informative than "great". Never buy or write reviews yourself.
  6. Keep facts identical everywhere. Address, phone and hours on your site, Maps and social profiles. Contradictions confuse readers and tools.
  7. Keep pages current. An old price or closed branch on a page damages trust.

Write the page like the question

Compare two openings for the same page.

Before. "We are passionate about your smile and committed to excellence in dental care."

After. "Example Dental Clinic in Jeddah offers teeth whitening, braces and routine check-ups for adults and children. Appointments are available six days a week."

The second one can be quoted as it stands. Use your own real facts, of course, not mine.

Think in neighbourhoods

Many customers search by area, not just city: "near me", or the district name. If you serve specific areas, say so on a page, with the real districts you serve, and show them on your Maps profile. Only list areas you actually cover.

Test it

Ask the question the way a customer would on two or three tools, on different days, and record who is named and why. My free visibility test prepares local questions by business type, with a link to try each one. For the idea of being recognised as one clear thing, see entity. For a multi-branch example, read the Point Market case study.

I cannot guarantee that any tool will name your business. These steps make your business clearer to customers and to the tools that read about it.
faq: Do I need a page for every city I serve?
Only for places where you actually operate or deliver. A genuine page for each real location is better than many near-identical pages.
Do reviews decide who gets named?
There is no official confirmation of that. Reviews matter to customers, and detailed honest ones help describe your business.
Is Google Maps enough without a website?
A complete Maps profile helps, but a website with clear facts gives tools and customers more to rely on.
